study.title: God is known in Judah
study.intro: Asaph's song celebrates God who dwells in Zion, breaks the weapons of war, judges from heaven and saves the lowly, so that even human wrath ends in His praise.
study.context: Psalm 76 is headed 'For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Psalm of Asaph. A song.' It belongs with the 'songs of Zion' such as Psalms 46 and 48, which praise God as the defender of His city. Many readers connect it with the sudden defeat of the Assyrian army outside Jerusalem in the days of Hezekiah (2 Kings 19:35), though the psalm itself names no battle. It moves from God's presence in Zion, to His victory, to His worldwide judgment, to a call for vows and tribute.
study.peopleNote: The heading names Asaph, the Levite worship leader appointed by David; the app has no Asaph profile yet, so no person card is linked. Verse 6 calls on the 'God of Jacob,' pointing back to the patriarch Jacob, who has a profile in the app. Planned paintings would show Zion's hills, broken weapons and quiet landscapes; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: Known in Judah
verses.heading: A name made great
verses.meaning: The heading names the choirmaster, stringed instruments and Asaph, and calls this a song. Then it opens: 'God is known in Judah; His name is great in Israel.' God has made Himself known among a particular people in a particular land. His name, meaning His revealed character and reputation, has grown great because of what He has done for them. Faith in the psalms is not vague spirituality but trust in a God who has acted in real history and let Himself be known.
verses.context: Psalm 76 shares themes with Psalms 46, 48 and 87, which celebrate God's protection of Jerusalem. Psalm 48:3 says God has made Himself known as a stronghold in Zion's citadels.
explore: Stringed instruments
Lyres and harps played with the fingers or a pick, used to accompany temple songs.
Name
In Hebrew thought a name expresses identity and reputation; God's name stands for all He has revealed of Himself.
verses.reflect: What has God done in your own story that has made Him 'known' to you?
verses.alt: Hill villages of Judah at dawn with terraced slopes and a road toward a walled city.

verses.title: Tent in Salem
verses.heading: God's chosen dwelling
verses.meaning: Verse 2 says: 'His tent is in Salem, His dwelling place in Zion.' Salem is an old, short name for Jerusalem, and it sounds like shalom, peace. God chose to place His presence among His people, first in a tent and then in the temple on Mount Zion. The word 'tent' recalls the tabernacle in the wilderness and suggests a God who comes close and camps with His people. The great God of verse 1 is not distant; He has an address among them.
verses.context: Melchizedek was king of Salem in Genesis 14:18. Zion was the hill David captured and where the ark was brought (2 Samuel 5:7). John 1:14 says the Word became flesh and 'tabernacled' among us.
explore: Salem
An ancient name for Jerusalem, related to the Hebrew word for peace, first seen with Melchizedek.
Dwelling place
The word can describe a lair or shelter, picturing God settled securely in Zion like a lion in its den.
verses.reflect: How does it comfort you that God chooses to dwell near His people rather than far away?
verses.alt: A plain tent of woven goat hair pitched on a rocky hill above a small city.

verses.title: Weapons shattered
verses.heading: The end of war's tools
verses.meaning: Verse 3 says: 'There He shattered the flaming arrows, the shield and sword and weapons of war. Selah.' At Zion, God broke the tools of the enemies who came against His city. Flaming arrows, shields and swords, every means of attack and defense, lie in pieces. The 'Selah' invites a pause to take it in. God's victory is not merely winning a battle but making war itself useless. It anticipates the day when He will end war entirely.
verses.context: Psalm 46:9 says God makes wars cease, breaking the bow and shattering the spear. Isaiah 2:4 foresees swords beaten into plowshares. Ephesians 6:16 speaks of the flaming arrows of the evil one.
explore: Flaming arrows
Literally 'flashes of the bow,' arrows that flew fast or were set alight to burn walls and gates.
Selah
A word of uncertain meaning in the Psalms, probably signalling a musical pause or a moment to reflect.
verses.reflect: What 'weapons' aimed at you do you need to trust God to break?
verses.alt: Broken bows, cracked shields and bent swords lying in grass below a city wall.

verses.title: Resplendent with light
verses.heading: More majestic than mountains
verses.meaning: Verse 4 turns to address God directly: 'You are resplendent with light, more majestic than mountains filled with game.' God shines with glory. The 'mountains filled with game' may picture the hills where predators hunt, or the enemy armies that came like beasts of prey. Either way, God is greater and more glorious than the most imposing heights and powers on earth. The psalmist answers God's victory not with pride in Israel but with wonder at God Himself.
verses.context: The phrase can be read 'mountains of prey,' a picture of enemy strongholds. Psalm 104:2 says God wraps Himself in light as with a garment. 1 Timothy 6:16 says He dwells in unapproachable light.
explore: Resplendent
Shining brilliantly; the Hebrew suggests being lit up or radiant with glory.
Game
Wild animals that are hunted, or the prey that hunting beasts seize in the hills.
verses.reflect: What draws your heart to wonder at God's glory more than at His gifts?
verses.alt: Sunlight breaking over rugged mountain ridges with deer on the far slopes.

verses.title: Their last sleep
verses.heading: The mighty are helpless
verses.meaning: Verse 5 says: 'The valiant lie plundered; they sleep their last sleep. No men of might could lift a hand.' The proud warriors who came to plunder are themselves plundered. They lie in the sleep of death, and the strongest among them cannot even raise a hand. Human strength, however impressive, is powerless when God acts. The verse is sobering: those who set themselves against God's purposes find their might suddenly gone.
verses.context: 2 Kings 19:35 tells how the Assyrian camp was struck in one night, and in the morning there were dead bodies everywhere. Isaiah 37:36 records the same event. Psalm 33:16 says a warrior is not delivered by great strength.
explore: Valiant
Literally 'stout of heart,' the brave and confident fighters of the enemy army.
Last sleep
A gentle way of describing death, the sleep from which they would not wake in this life.
verses.reflect: Where are you tempted to trust strength or skill more than God?
verses.alt: An empty battlefield at dawn with abandoned spears and quiet mist.

verses.title: Horse and rider stunned
verses.heading: The God of Jacob rebukes
verses.meaning: Verse 6 says: 'At Your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both horse and rider lie stunned.' God does not need weapons; a word of rebuke is enough. Chariot horses and their riders, the most feared military force of the day, fall into a deep stupor. The title 'God of Jacob' reminds Israel that this is the same faithful God who cared for their forefather. This echoes the song of Moses after the Red Sea, when horse and rider were thrown into the sea.
verses.context: Exodus 15:1 sings that the LORD has hurled horse and rider into the sea. Psalm 20:7 says some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD.
explore: Rebuke
A sharp word of command or correction; when God rebukes, creation and enemies obey.
Stunned
Cast into a deep, heavy sleep, the same word used of Adam's deep sleep in Genesis 2:21.
verses.reflect: What would it mean for you to trust God's word more than any visible 'horse and chariot'?
verses.alt: Riderless horses standing still beside overturned chariots on a dusty plain.

verses.title: Who can stand?
verses.heading: God alone to be feared
verses.meaning: Verse 7 says: 'You alone are to be feared. When You are angry, who can stand before You?' After seeing God's power, the right response is awe. The armies that frightened Israel are nothing compared to God. His anger against evil is real, and no one can stand against it on their own strength. Yet the fear of God frees us from lesser fears. When we stand in awe of Him, threats from people lose their grip on us.
verses.context: Nahum 1:6 asks who can stand before His indignation. Malachi 3:2 asks who can endure the day of His coming. Romans 5:1-2 says through Christ we now stand in grace.
explore: Fear of God
Reverent awe that recognizes God's holiness and power, leading to worship and obedience.
Stand
To hold one's ground in judgment or battle; no one can do so against God by their own merit.
verses.reflect: How could a deeper awe of God loosen the hold that other fears have on you?
verses.alt: A lone figure in a head cloth kneeling on a rock beneath a vast stormy sky.

verses.title: From heaven
verses.heading: The earth falls silent
verses.meaning: Verse 8 says: 'From heaven You pronounced judgment, and the earth feared and was still.' God's verdict comes from His throne above. When He speaks, the noisy, warring earth goes silent in fear. The armies stop, the nations hush, and creation waits. There is a silence that comes from awe, when every protest and boast ends because God has spoken. That stillness is also an invitation for us to quiet our hearts before Him.
verses.context: Psalm 46:10 says, 'Be still, and know that I am God.' Habakkuk 2:20 says let all the earth be silent before Him. Zechariah 2:13 calls all people to be still before the LORD.
explore: Pronounced judgment
Literally 'caused judgment to be heard,' God announcing His verdict for all to hear.
Still
Quiet and at rest, like a land after war has ended and the noise of battle has stopped.
verses.reflect: When was the last time you were quiet enough before God simply to listen?
verses.alt: A wide valley in perfect stillness under clearing clouds after a storm.

verses.title: To save the lowly
verses.heading: Judgment that rescues
verses.meaning: Verse 9 continues: 'when God rose up to judge, to save all the lowly of the earth. Selah.' God's judgment has a purpose: rescue. He rises up not only to punish oppressors but to save the humble and afflicted everywhere. The 'lowly of the earth' are the poor, the weak and those crushed by others' power. God's justice is good news for them. The Selah invites us to pause and see that judgment and salvation belong together in God's heart.
verses.context: Psalm 72:4 says the king will vindicate the afflicted. Isaiah 11:4 says the Messiah will judge the poor with righteousness. Luke 1:52 says God has brought down rulers and exalted the humble.
explore: Rose up
God acting decisively, as a judge rising from his seat to give a verdict.
Lowly
The humble, poor and afflicted, who depend on God because they have no other power.
verses.reflect: Who are the 'lowly' around you, and how might you share in God's care for them?
verses.alt: A poor family by a simple stone house looking up as morning light reaches them.

verses.title: Wrath turned to praise
verses.heading: God uses even human anger
verses.meaning: Verse 10 says: 'Even the wrath of man shall praise You; with the survivors of wrath You will clothe Yourself.' Human rage against God and His people cannot defeat Him; in the end it only displays His glory. God turns even hostile anger into an occasion for praise. The second line is difficult; it may mean God wears the remnant of wrath like a belt, holding it in control. Either way, no human fury escapes His sovereign purpose.
verses.context: Genesis 50:20 says what others meant for evil, God meant for good. Acts 4:27-28 says those who opposed Jesus did what God's hand had decided beforehand. Romans 8:28 says God works all things for good for those who love Him.
explore: Wrath of man
Human fury and hostility, especially of enemies who rage against God and His people.
Clothe Yourself
Literally 'gird Yourself,' wrapping something around oneself like a belt, a sign of control.
verses.reflect: What hostility or anger in your life might God be able to turn toward His praise?
verses.alt: A storm cloud passing over hills with a bright band of light breaking at its edge.

verses.title: Make and fulfill vows
verses.heading: Tribute to the awesome God
verses.meaning: Verse 11 says: 'Make and fulfill your vows to the LORD your God; let all the neighboring lands bring tribute to Him who is to be feared.' The right response to God's rescue is commitment. Israel is told to make promises to God and to keep them. Even surrounding nations should bring gifts, recognizing His greatness. Worship that only feels grateful but never commits falls short; real thanks moves us to give ourselves and our gifts to God.
verses.context: Ecclesiastes 5:4 says when you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it. Psalm 116:14 says, 'I will fulfill my vows to the LORD.' Isaiah 18:7 pictures gifts brought to Mount Zion.
explore: Vow
A solemn promise made to God, often to offer a sacrifice or service in thanks for His help.
Tribute
A gift brought by a lesser nation to a greater king, acknowledging his rule.
verses.reflect: Is there a promise you have made to God that you need to keep?
verses.alt: Villagers climbing a hill path carrying baskets of grain and jars as offerings.

verses.title: Princes humbled
verses.heading: Feared by the kings of the earth
verses.meaning: Verse 12 ends: 'He breaks the spirits of princes; He is feared by the kings of the earth.' The rulers who seem untouchable are humbled by God. He can cut off their proud breath, and kings across the earth tremble before Him. The psalm that began with God known in Judah ends with God feared worldwide. No power is beyond His reach, which is a warning to the proud and a comfort to the lowly He came to save.
verses.context: Psalm 2:10-11 warns kings to serve the LORD with fear. Daniel 4:37 has Nebuchadnezzar confess that God humbles the proud. Revelation 19:16 calls Christ King of kings and Lord of lords.
explore: Breaks the spirits
Literally 'cuts off the breath,' humbling the pride and arrogance of rulers.
Kings of the earth
All the rulers of the nations, who must one day bow before God's authority.
verses.reflect: How does knowing God is over every ruler shape how you view world events today?
verses.alt: A deserted royal hall with an empty throne and a crown set down on the step.
